theme.text: The surah is a complete statement of tawḥīd: who God is (One, al-Ṣamad) and what He is not (not begetting, not begotten, without equal).
theme.source: General tafsir: al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī on Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ

theme.text: The Prophet ﷺ said that this surah equals a third of the Qurʾān.
theme.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5013, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī

theme.text: Scholars explain the "third" in different ways. One common explanation: the Qurʾān's content falls into rulings, narratives, and the description of God, and this surah gathers the third kind.
theme.scholar: Reported in al-Qurṭubī's tafsir among other explanations

revelation.text: Most scholars count the surah as Makkan; others count it as Madinan. The difference follows the reports about who asked the question that it answers (see verse 1, reason for revelation).
revelation.scholar: Both positions are discussed by Ibn ʿĀshūr
revelation.source: Ibn ʿĀshūr, al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr, introduction to 112

claims.text: al-Masad names a man by his kunya, Abū Lahab, and says his wealth and what he earned will not save him. al-Ikhlāṣ follows with the One who has no lineage at all and needs nothing. Human lineage and wealth fail; God is beyond both.
al-Ikhlāṣ, al-Falaq and al-Nās all open with the command "qul" (say). The Prophet ﷺ would recite the three together before sleeping.
claims.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Book of the Virtues of the Qurʾān, from ʿĀʾisha

claims.text: al-Ikhlāṣ first establishes who God is; al-Falaq and al-Nās then turn to seeking refuge in Him. Knowing the One comes before asking Him for protection.

claim.text: No ring structure is claimed. The word aḥad closes both verse 1 and verse 4, which frames the surah, but four short verses are too few to establish a ring.

meanings: to state a view or belief
words.used: "Say!" A command to speak out loud.

why.text: Imperative form. The command is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and through him to everyone who recites it.

words.lexSource: al-Rāghib, al-Mufradāt, entry q-w-l; Lane's Lexicon, q-w-l

words.used: Both readings are valid: "He" (the Lord they asked about) or "the matter is".

why.text: The pronoun can point back to the one asked about, or it can be the pronoun of the matter, which announces that a weighty statement follows.
Scholars differ on whether the name is derived (from ilāh, "one who is worshipped") or is a proper name with no derivation. Both views are old and the study does not choose between them.
why.scholar: al-Rāghib discusses the derivation; the disagreement is reported among grammarians

words.rootTr: w-ḥ-d (the hamza replaces an original wāw)
words.used: One: unique, with no second and no parts.

why.text: In an affirmative sentence, aḥad in this absolute sense is used only of God. Elsewhere it mostly appears after a negation, meaning "anyone".

words.lexSource: al-Rāghib, al-Mufradāt, entry aḥad; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs, w-ḥ-d

layers.reading: "He" refers to the Lord they asked about
layers.translation: Say: He is Allah, the One.

claim.text: huwa points back to the one being asked about.

layers.reading: "He" is the pronoun of the matter
layers.translation: Say: The truth is this: Allah is One.

claim.text: huwa is ḍamīr al-shaʾn, and "Allāhu aḥad" is the statement it announces.

linguistics.text: aḥad, not wāḥid. wāḥid can start a count (one, two, three), so it leaves room for a second. aḥad, used as an attribute of God, rules out any second and any division.
aḥad is indefinite (aḥadun, not al-aḥad). The indefinite can suggest a oneness that belongs to no category: He is not "the one" of a known class.
The command "qul" is kept in the recited text. The reciter repeats what was given to say, which marks the words as a message passed on rather than something composed.
All four verses end on -ad (aḥad, ṣamad, yūlad, aḥad). The closing dāl is a qalqala letter, so each verse ends with a short, firm stop.

tafsir.text: The verse declares that God is One, with no partner, no equal and no division. It is the core statement the rest of the surah explains.

narration.text: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb reported that the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Describe your Lord's lineage to us," and God revealed this surah.
narration.source: Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī, Book of Tafsīr, on 112; Musnad Aḥmad

grading.text: al-Tirmidhī also gives the report without Ubayy (mursal, from Abū al-ʿĀliya) and says that version is more correct. The connected chain includes Abū Jaʿfar al-Rāzī, about whom the hadith critics differ. Later graders disagree on whether it is ḥasan or weak.

disagreement.text: Other reports say the question came from Jews of Madinah, not from the Quraysh. al-Ṭabarī collects reports on both sides. This is the source of the Makkan or Madinan disagreement.

why.text: See verse 1 for the disagreement on derivation.

meanings: to aim for, to turn to (qaṣd)
the master to whom people turn in their needs
the master perfect in his mastery
the one who remains, the Everlasting
words.used: All of these meanings are carried. The word is not reduced to one.

why.text: Ibn Fāris gives the root two core senses: aiming for something, and solidity. The early exegetes explain al-Ṣamad with several meanings built on these, and al-Ṭabarī collects their reports.
why.source: Maqāyīs al-Lugha, ṣ-m-d; Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 112:2

words.lexSource: Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs, ṣ-m-d; Lane's Lexicon, ṣ-m-d

layers.translation: Allah is the One to whom all turn in their needs.

claim.text: From the root sense of aiming for and turning to.
claim.scholar: Reported from early exegetes in al-Ṭabarī

layers.translation: Allah is the Self-Sufficient, with no hollowness and no need.

claim.text: From the root sense of solidity: one who has no inside that needs filling, who neither eats nor drinks.
claim.scholar: Reported from early exegetes in al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr
claim.source: Jāmiʿ al-Bayān and Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr, on 112:2

layers.translation: Allah is the Master, perfect in His mastery.

claim.text: Reported from Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa.
claim.scholar: Ibn ʿAbbās, as reported by Ibn Kathīr

layers.translation: Allah is the Everlasting, who remains after His creation.

claim.text: Reported from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Qatāda.
claim.scholar: al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Qatāda, as reported by Ibn Kathīr

linguistics.text: Both parts of the sentence are definite (Allāh, al-Ṣamad). In Arabic rhetoric this pattern can express restriction: Allah alone is al-Ṣamad.
The name Allāh is repeated instead of using the pronoun ("He is al-Ṣamad"). Each verse then stands as a full statement about God by name.
There is no "and" between verse 1 and verse 2. The second sentence follows directly, as if it explains the first.
al-Ṣamad occurs only here in the Qurʾān. One rare word holds meanings that would otherwise need several (master, self-sufficient, everlasting).

tafsir.text: Everything depends on God and He depends on nothing. The several explanations of al-Ṣamad do not contradict one another, and many exegetes accept them together.

asbab.note: No separate narration for this verse. See verse 1 for the surah as a whole.

meanings: not (negates the past; puts the verb in the jussive)

why.text: lam with the present-form verb gives a past negation: "did not".

words.used: To beget: to have a child.

why.text: Active voice: God is the subject. It denies that He has a child.

words.lexSource: Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs, w-l-d; Lane's Lexicon, w-l-d

why.text: wa joins the second negation to the first.

meanings: to be begotten, to be born
words.used: To be begotten: to have a parent.

why.text: Passive voice of the same root. It denies that He has a parent or origin.

verses.literal: Not [has He] begotten, and not [has He] been begotten.

layers.translation: He has not begotten, and He has not been begotten.

claim.text: The plain meaning of lam with the jussive.

layers.translation: He never begets, and He was never begotten.

claim.text: Since the verse answers a question about God's nature, the past negation can be read as covering all time.

linguistics.text: "Has not begotten" comes before "has not been begotten". People had claimed that God has children; nobody claimed that He was born. The verse answers the claim that was made first.
linguistics.source: A common explanation in tafsir; a named source is still needed

linguistics.text: One root, two voices (yalid / yūlad). The pair closes off both directions: no descendants and no ancestors.
The verse has two balanced halves of the same length and pattern: lam yalid / wa-lam yūlad.

tafsir.text: God has no child and no parent. This answers those who said God has a son or daughters, as other verses also do (for example 6:101 and 19:88–92).

asbab.note: No separate narration for this verse. See verse 1 for the surah as a whole.

why.text: Past negation, joined to the previous verse.
kāna is used here as a linking verb. Its subject is aḥad and its predicate is kufuwan.
li (for, to) with the pronoun hu (Him).

meanings: a peer in rank or standing

why.text: kufuʾ is a match or peer, the same word family as kafāʾa, equality of standing.

words.lexSource: Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs, k-f-ʾ; Lane's Lexicon, k-f-ʾ

why.text: After a negation, aḥad covers every possible individual: no one at all.

verses.literal: And not has been for Him [an] equal, [any] one.

layers.reading: kufuwan is the predicate, aḥad is the subject
layers.translation: And there has never been anyone equal to Him.

claim.text: The usual parsing: the predicate kufuwan is placed before the subject aḥad.

layers.reading: lahu is the predicate, kufuwan describes the state
layers.translation: And no one has ever stood toward Him as an equal.

claim.text: Some grammarians allow kufuwan as a circumstantial (ḥāl). Confirm the source before keeping this layer.
claim.scholar: Reported in works of iʿrāb, possibly al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī, al-Durr al-Maṣūn

linguistics.text: lahu (to Him) is placed before kufuwan (an equal), although such a phrase would normally come later. It is fronted because the point is to deny an equal to God specifically.
kufuw, not mithl (likeness) or nidd (rival). kufuw speaks of equal rank, so the verse denies anyone who could stand at God's level, not only anyone who resembles Him.
The surah opens its statement with aḥad (verse 1) and closes with aḥad (verse 4). The first affirms He is One; the last denies that anyone is like Him.

tafsir.text: Nothing and no one is equal or comparable to God, in His essence, attributes or actions. Compare 42:11: "There is nothing like Him."

asbab.note: No separate narration for this verse. See verse 1 for the surah as a whole.
